takeaway: Massive transfusion: citrate binds calcium, giving hypocalcaemia, and hyperkalaemia occurs too; together they cause ECG and rhythm changes.

question.text: An 18-year-old shot and transfused 12 units of blood shows ECG changes. Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely?

lines.text: A young man is shot and needs twelve units of blood.
That is a massive transfusion, so the blood bags matter.
Donor blood contains citrate, the anticoagulant, which binds the patient's calcium.
Potassium rises as well, so he is likely hyperkalaemic.
Both can cause cardiac rhythm abnormalities.
That is why the anaesthetist sees the ECG change.
lines.say: (sigh) That is why the anaesthetist sees the ECG change.

lines.text: So: low calcium and high potassium.
